Now let me compile the notes verse by verse from the materials gathered. I could not get new pages for Catholic, Orthodox, or modern scholarship sources (search/fetch limits reached), so I will note those gaps.

---

## Proverbs 14 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1: "Every wise woman builds her house, but a foolish one tears it down with her own hands."

- **Traditional reading (Guzik / Enduring Word):** Wisdom is constructive; folly is inherently destructive. The woman of a home has tremendous power to make it a better or worse place. Many homes have been made by a godly, wise woman who looks after the home and builds it. Charles Bridges adds that the foolish woman's idleness, waste, and love of pleasure tears her house down — "it would have been a sad result if this had been done by an enemy. But it is the … undoing of her own hands." Trapp: "As the husband is as the head … so she is as the hands into which [the sinews] flow." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The Hebrew word *chakhmoth* may be pointed differently to read *chokhmoth* ("wisdom"), making it "The wisdom of women buildeth their house" — an abstract parallel to "folly" in the second line. Foolish, unprincipled women ruin their families materially and morally by bad management or evil doings. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

- **Gill (Baptist):** Not only by fruitfulness (as Leah and Rachel built Israel) but by good housewifery, prudent economy, guiding affairs with discretion, and bringing up children in the fear of the Lord. Gill also sees Christ typologically: Christ as "Wisdom" builds His house, the church. Gill further applies it polemically: the apostate church of Rome (as the "foolish woman") pulls down the true church with false doctrines and idolatry. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 2: "He who walks in uprightness fears the LORD, but the one who is devious in his ways despises Him."

- **Guzik:** Upright walk demonstrates fear of the LORD. The NT attitude: Christ has made us new creatures; our duty is to walk in that uprightness. The disobedient man despises God's authority — it is deep-seated rebellion, not mere weakness. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary / Ellicott:** The outward conduct shows the inward feeling. Delitzsch renders it, "He walketh in his uprightness who feareth Jahve, and perverse in his ways is he that despiseth him." The Vulgate gives a different turn: the upright man who fears the Lord *is despised by* him who walks in the path of shame — intimating the hatred sinners feel for the godly (cf. John 15:18-21). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 3: "The proud speech of a fool brings a rod to his back, but the lips of the wise protect them."

- **Guzik:** The "rod of pride" is in the fool's own mouth — he is his own worst enemy. Waltke: "The fool's pride finds a rod in his mouth that lashes himself … and others." The wise are preserved by their own wise words. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The Hebrew *choter* ("rod" or "shoot," also in Isaiah 11:1) pictures a growth of vaunting and conceit from the arrogant fool's mouth, accompanied by insolence toward others, for which he is often chastised. St. Gregory applied this to haughty preachers who "know how to smite sharply, but not to sympathize with humility." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

- **Gill:** The proud tongue is not only a rod to others but a scourge to oneself — the cause of evil coming upon the fool. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 4: "Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty, but an abundant harvest comes through the strength of the ox."

- **Guzik / Enduring Word:** Where no work is being accomplished, there is no mess — but also no increase. The mess an ox brings is worth it. Kidner: "Orderliness can reach the point of sterility. This proverb is not a plea for slovenliness … but for the readiness to accept upheaval, and a mess to clear up, as the price of growth." Application to church life: hyper-regulation and suspicion of any "mess" among believers creates an environment where there is little spiritual increase. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Without oxen (cattle) to labor, the crib is empty — there is nothing to put in the granary. The means must be adapted to the end. The "ploughing ox" is the type of industry; where agricultural work is diligently carried on, large returns are secured. Not an exhortation to kindness to animals (which would make no antithesis). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

- **Gill (Baptist):** Oxen are an emblem of faithful, laborious ministers of the Gospel. The ox was one of the cherubim emblems; ministers are "seers, overseers" who need good sight to search the Scriptures and look to their flock. Where there are no such ministers, there is no spiritual food for souls (a famine of the Word). Through the unwearied labors of Gospel ministers and God's blessing, there is much spiritual increase. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 5: "An honest witness does not deceive, but a dishonest witness pours forth lies."

- **Guzik:** A straightforward statement with spiritual application — Jesus calls His followers to be His witnesses (Acts 1:8). A faithful witness simply tells the truth. Poole adds that one who has "debauched his conscience by daily lying" is thereby prepared for false witness-bearing. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** A repetition of Proverbs 12:17. A faithful witness cannot be induced to swerve by threat or bribe. The false witness "breatheth forth" lies — as if naturally, with no compulsion. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

- **Gill:** The character of a faithful witness is given to Christ (Revelation 1:5), who is truth itself and cannot lie. One who accustoms himself to lying in private will become a false witness in public — lesser sins lead to greater ones. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 6: "A mocker seeks wisdom and finds none, but knowledge comes easily to the discerning."

- **Guzik:** When someone seeks wisdom and does not find it, it is evidence they are likely a scoffer — their pursuit is cynical and superficial. Clarke: "Such may seek wisdom; but he never can find it, because he does not seek it where it is to be found; neither in the teaching of God's Spirit, nor in the revelation of his will." For the sincere seeker, knowledge is easy (cf. Matthew 7:7). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** True wisdom is not won by those who are too conceited to receive instruction. This is especially true of the knowledge of divine things, which scorners never really acquire. Cf. Wisdom 1:4, "Into a malicious soul wisdom shall not enter." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 7: "Stay away from a foolish man; you will gain no knowledge from his speech."

- **Guzik:** The fool and the wise man can almost always be known by their words. Avoid the presence of a foolish man. Ross: "One cannot increase in knowledge by associating with a fool — nothing comes from nothing." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** There is ambiguity in the Hebrew *minneged* ("from before" / "over against"). The AV renders it as an injunction to turn away from a fool when you perceive you can do him no good. The RV: "Go into the presence of a foolish man, and thou shalt not perceive in him the lips of knowledge." Nowack explains: "Leave the presence of a fool, and you carry nothing away with you; after all your intercourse … you quit without having gained any advance in true knowledge." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 8: "The wisdom of the prudent is to discern his way, but the folly of fools deceives them."

- **Guzik:** The prudent person carefully considers and understands his way — the path, their point upon it, and their progress. Poole: "It consists not in vain speculations, nor in a curious prying into other men's matters … but in a diligent study of his own duty, and of the way to true and eternal happiness." The folly of fools is deceit — their attraction is based on deceit, like bait hiding a hook. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** This may also refer to choosing a calling or occupation that best suits one's capabilities, station, and opportunities. The folly of fools is deceit of others — stupid persons try to cheat others but are sure to be detected, and the fraud recoils on themselves. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

- **Gill:** What the Holy Ghost calls "folly" is itself "deceit" — it is science falsely so called (1 Corinthians 3:19). It lies in tricking and deceiving, and the issue is deceiving both others and themselves. Gill applies this to the "man of sin" (the papacy) deceiving with sorceries and lying wonders. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 9: "Fools mock the making of amends, but goodwill is found among the upright."

- **Guzik:** Fools think sin is a light thing, worthy to be mocked. Clarke: "He that makes a sport of sinning, will find it no sport to suffer the vengeance of an eternal fire." Among the upright there is favor with God and man. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary (important translation issue):** The Hebrew *asham* means both "sin" and "sin offering." The AV rendering requires a violent grammatical anomaly (singular verb with plural noun). Better: "The sin offering of fools mocks them" — i.e., it is vain for fools to seek God's favor by ceremonial observances when their heart is wrong (cf. Proverbs 15:8; 21:27; Sirach 31:18-19). The disposition of the heart conditions the acceptableness of worship. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

- **Gill:** Similarly notes the alternative rendering "sin offering," and applies it polemically: the sin offering/sacrifice of Christ is mocked by false teachers, denied, and exposed to contempt by Papists through the "bloodless sacrifice of the mass" and works of supererogation. Alternatively, "sin makes a mock of fools" — it deceives them by promising pleasure, profit, or honor but giving none. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 10: "The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares in its joy."

- **Guzik:** There is pain and bitterness enough for every heart, but it is difficult for anyone else to know the pain of another's heart. The same is true of joy — it can be difficult for anyone else to truly share. Bridges: "No less personal is the heart's joy. It lies deep within. Michal could understand David's bravery, but not his joy." Spurgeon listed joys a stranger cannot share: sin forgiven, sin conquered, restored relationship with God, accepted service, answered prayer, usefulness for God, peace in trouble, and highest of all, communion with God. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Neither our joys nor sorrows can be wholly shared with another. But we can turn to the God-Man Jesus, who knows our frame, wept human tears, bore our sorrows, and has taken His human experience with Him into heaven. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 11: "The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish."

- **Guzik:** The wicked boasts of his great house and looks down on his upright neighbor in only a tent. Yet the tent of the upright is more secure than the house of the wicked. Waltke notes: "The tent … refers to a nomadic tent. It is a bell tent, supported in the middle by a wooden pole and composed of several dark, goatskin curtains." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Sinners take great pains to increase material prosperity and leave heirs, but Providence defeats their efforts. Good men do their duty, leave anxious care for the future, and God prospers them beyond all they thought or wished. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 12: "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death."

- **Guzik:** One of the chapter's most important proverbs. What seems right to a man isn't necessarily right — it can be the way of death. Waltke: "The safety and destiny of a road are not always as they appear (Matt. 7:13-14). The deceptive road leads as certainly to death as the plainly marked one." This makes plain our need for revelation from God — we cannot entirely trust our own judgment. Repeated at Proverbs 16:25. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** This warns against following a perverted or uninstructed conscience. Conscience needs to be informed by God's Word to be a safe guide. Warped by prejudice, weakened by disuse and disobedience, it loses all power of moral judgment, and the man following a false light goes headlong to destruction (cf. Romans 1:28; 1 Timothy 4:2). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

- **Gill (Baptist/Reformed):** The way of sin promises carnal pleasure and has much company, but leads to destruction. The way of the hypocrite and Pharisee who trusts his own righteousness and despises Christ's righteousness also seems right but ends in death. Even Popery, through pomp and lying miracles, seems right but leads to eternal death. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/proverbs-14.html

- **Gospel Coalition (Tim Keller):** Keller notes how Proverbs only gives up its meaning cumulatively. Proverbs 14:12 appears to apply to the fool, but when repeated at 16:25 it is applied to "a man" — anyone. "But the way of destruction can appear right not just to a fool, but sometimes to anyone … Even if you follow the way of wisdom to the 'T' … sometimes your life can still blow up! This is a broken world." — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/proverbs-community-and-the-culture/

- **Ligonier (Reformed):** Gene Edward Veith notes that this verse teaches that our own mind, apart from God's Word, will lead us astray, even if our idea seems to make sense. — https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/train-child

---

### v. 13: "Even in laughter the heart may ache, and joy may end in sorrow."

- **Guzik:** Outward laughter may mask great sorrow. Poole: "The design of the proverb is to declare the vanity of all worldly joys and comforts, and to teach men moderation in them, and to persuade us to seek for more solid and durable joys." Laughter and mirth may do more than mask sorrow — they may end in grief. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** Recalls Lucretius: "From the very fountain of delights there rises something bitter that chokes us even among the flowers." Joy and sorrow are strangely intermingled in this mortal life. The LXX inadvertently introduced a negative giving the opposite sense: "In joys there is no admixture of sorrow, but the final joy cometh unto grief." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 14: "The backslider in heart receives the fill of his own ways, but a good man is rewarded for his ways."

- **Spurgeon (Baptist, sermon on this verse):** A common principle: men are affected by the course they pursue — their own conduct comes home to them. The backslider "slides back with an easy, effortless motion, softly, quietly, perhaps unsuspected by himself or anybody else." Like two sponges — one in foul water, one in pure — each is filled with what it lies in. "What a man is by sin or by grace will be the cause of his sorrow or of his satisfaction." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/proverbs-14.html

- **Guzik:** "Filled with his own ways" means having his soul saturated with folly, sin, and disappointment. Bridges cautions: "Every spot does not mean that you have leprosy. Every sin does not indicate that you are a backslider." Morgan: "Whatever may be within a man, in the deepest region of his personality, will sooner or later be wrought out into actual experience and visibility." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Parker's People's Bible:** Backsliding takes place in the heart, not in the foot. The backslider shall be "filled with the fruit which he has coveted … mocked and taunted by the spirit of judgment." The good man "shall be satisfied from himself" — from the treasure within, from remembered prayers and recollected promises. "Take from a good man his money, his health, his society, yea, his very books … yet his memory abides, a treasure-house well filled." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jpb/proverbs-14.html

- **Pulpit Commentary (translation note):** Delitzsch and others read "a good man from his own deeds" (repeating the verb from the first clause). The Vulgate reads "and over him shall be the good man." LXX: "and a good man from his thoughts." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 15: "The simple man believes every word, but the prudent man watches his steps."

- **Guzik:** The "simple" lack wisdom and have little ability to discern truth from falsehood — they believe everyone, especially if they seem sincere. Bridges: "To believe every word of God is faith. To believe every word of man is credulity." The prudent give more consideration to their own steps. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The credulous fool believes all he hears without proof or examination; having no fixed principles, he is at the mercy of any adviser. It is often remarked how credulous unbelievers in supernaturalism are — they refuse to credit Christ's history but pin their faith on some insufficiently supported philosophical theory. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 16: "A wise man fears and turns from evil, but a fool is careless and reckless."

- **Guzik:** The wise man appreciates evil for what it is and keeps far from it — he does not overestimate his own strength in resisting evil. The fool rages with uncontrolled temper and outbursts, yet is self-confident. "The self-confidence of fools is a mystery and a marvel." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The wise man fears the evil that lurks in everything and examines actions by the standard of religion. The fool easily falls into a rage, has no control over himself, and is confident in his own wisdom — in contrast to the wise man who has trust in God and is calm and thoughtful (Isaiah 30:15). The Hebrew *mithabber* means "to be excited," "to be in a passion." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 17: "A quick-tempered man acts foolishly, and a devious man is hated."

- **Guzik:** The quick-tempered man acts out his foolishness. Clarke notes the Hebrew *ketsar appayim* literally means "short of nostrils" — because when a man is angry his nose contracts. The man of wicked intentions is understood to be untrustworthy and therefore hated. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The contrast is with the man "slow to anger" (v.29). In haste and passion, a man does things which in calmer moments he must see are foolish. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/proverbs-14.html

---

### v. 18: "The simple inherit folly, but the prudent are crowned with knowledge."

- **Guzik:** As one gains an inheritance as something due, so the simple inherit folly — for those who willfully reject wisdom, folly is their due. The prudent enjoy the benefits of wisdom; knowledge sits upon them as a graceful and noble crown. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

---

### v. 19: "The evil bow before the good, and the wicked at the gates of the righteous."

- **Guzik:** Though in this present age the evil often seem to win, ultimately evil will bow in submission before the good. Ross: "Ultimately the wicked will acknowledge and serve the righteous. The figure used here is of a conquered people kneeling before their victors awaiting their commands." Bridges notes examples: the Egyptians and Joseph's brothers bowed before Joseph; Pharaoh bowed before Moses; the saints will judge the world (1 Corinthians 6:2). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

---

### v. 20: "The poor man is hated even by his neighbor, but many are those who love the rich."

- **Guzik:** An honest observation about the benefits of wealth — the poor don't have as many friends, and even their neighbor may hate them. The friends of the rich might be insincere, but there are more of them. Bridges: "This is a humbling but common illustration of natural selfishness … But Jesus was deliberately the poor man's friend. How endearing is Jesus' love!" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

---

### v. 21: "He who despises his neighbor sins, but blessed is he who shows kindness to the poor."

- **Guzik:** Men and women are made in the image of God; to despise one's neighbor is to sin (Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 22:39). The generous heart is the happy heart. Whoever shows mercy to the poor should never do so in a superior manner that would show they despise the poor they claim to help. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

---

### v. 22: "Do not those who contrive evil go astray? But those who plan goodness find loving devotion and faithfulness."

- **Guzik:** Even the plotting and devising of evil leads us astray — God cares about heart and mind as well as outward actions (Matthew 5:21-32). Trapp on "devise evil": "Hebrew, That plough it and plot it, that dig it and delve it, that whet their wits and beat their brains about it — do not these err?" Bridges: "Wicked as it is to do evil, it is far more wicked to plot evil." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

---

### v. 23: "There is profit in all labor, but mere talk leads only to poverty."

- **Guzik:** Hard work is always rewarded — if not in immediate profit, then in character and God's reward. Idle chatter distracts from labor and leads to poverty. Ross: "People should be more afraid of idle talk than of hard work." Trapp: "Great talkers are do-littles, for the most part." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

---

### v. 24: "The crown of the wise is their wealth, but the effort of fools is folly."

- **Guzik:** Solomon knew riches can come through wisdom and hard work; in such cases, riches are like a crown — both evidence and reward of wisdom. For those who reject wisdom, the only crown they get is more folly — their foolishness is multiplied. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

---

### v. 25: "A truthful witness saves lives, but one who utters lies is deceitful."

- **Guzik:** Truth brings light, blessing, and freedom on an everyday level; where lies and false reports dominate, souls will be in danger. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- (The Enduring Word page was truncated after this point, so verses 26–35 are drawn from the summary material and Gill/Pulpit excerpts.)

---

### v. 26: "He who fears the LORD is secure in confidence, and his children shall have a place of refuge."

- **Guzik (summary):** Reverence for the LORD provides strong confidence and shelter for one's children. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

---

### v. 27: "The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, turning a man from the snares of death."

- **Guzik:** One might think fear always leads to less life, but proper fear of the LORD is rooted in understanding who God is and who we are in relation to Him — that itself is like a fountain of life, protecting from the snares of death. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

---

### v. 28: "A large population is a king's splendor, but a lack of subjects is a prince's ruin."

- **Traditional reading:** A thriving population honors a king; dwindling subjects ruin a ruler. — https://biblehub.com/proverbs/14.htm

---

### v. 29: "A patient man has great understanding, but a quick-tempered man promotes folly."

- **Guzik:** There is great wisdom in the ability to control one's response to provoking situations. Being quick to wrath brings many regrets. The impulsive, uncontrolled person who quickly reacts without thinking lives in a way that exalts foolishness. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

---

### v. 30: "A tranquil heart is life to the body, but envy rots the bones."

- **Guzik (summary):** A calm heart nourishes the body; envy rots the bones. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

---

### v. 31: "Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker, but whoever is kind to the needy honors Him."

- **Guzik (summary):** Oppressing the poor insults their Maker; caring for the needy honors Him. This links the treatment of the poor directly with one's relationship to God, since the poor are made in His image. — https://biblehub.com/proverbs/14.htm

---

### v. 32: "The wicked man is thrown down by his own sin, but the righteous man has a refuge even in death."

- **Precept Austin (summary):** The wicked are toppled by their own sin, yet the righteous have refuge even in death. This is a remarkable OT statement about the security of the righteous beyond the grave. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/proverbs_illustrations_2

- (I was unable to reach specific Catholic, Orthodox, or denominational pages on this verse due to search limits. Traditional Protestant readings take this as pointing toward confidence in God through death; Catholic and Orthodox readings would likely connect it with hope of resurrection.)

---

### v. 33: "Wisdom rests in the heart of the discerning; even among fools she is known."

- **Guzik:** Wisdom finds a suitable home in the heart of those who have understanding — it isn't a temporary visitor; it comes and *rests* in the heart. Bridges: "True wisdom sets its throne in the heart." The BSB footnote indicates an alternative reading: "but what is in the heart of fools is made known." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

---

### v. 34: "Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a disgrace to any people."

- **Guzik:** Because righteousness follows God's will and God's way, it will always exalt a person, family, neighborhood, city, state, or nation — both through natural consequences and God's active blessing. Military might, economic prosperity, and cultural influence may seem to exalt a nation, but none match righteousness. "The most patriotic thing a citizen might do is repent of their sin and … pursue God's righteousness in their life." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-14/

- (This verse is frequently cited across traditions in discussions of civil governance. I could not obtain pages from specific denominational sites, but it is widely used by both conservative Evangelicals to argue for national moral renewal and by mainline Protestants in social-justice contexts.)

---

### v. 35: "A king delights in a wise servant, but his anger falls on the shameful."

- **Guzik (summary):** Wisdom applies to civic life and leadership; a ruler values wise service and punishes shameful conduct. — https://biblehub.com/proverbs/14.htm

---

## Denominational Distinctives Observed

**Baptist (Gill, Spurgeon):** Gill's commentary (1746) is distinctively Baptist in its strong anti-Catholic polemic, repeatedly identifying "the apostate church of Rome" with the foolish woman, false teachers, and the "man of sin." Spurgeon's sermon on v.14 emphasizes personal experience of grace — the backslider slides "softly, quietly, perhaps unsuspected" and the good man is satisfied "from himself" (the indwelling grace of God). Both show the Baptist emphasis on regenerate church membership and personal holiness.

**Reformed / Presbyterian (Ligonier, Gospel Coalition):** Keller's TGC article highlights the cumulative reading of Proverbs — no single proverb gives the whole picture; they must be read together as a community under mentorship. Ligonier emphasizes Proverbs 14:12 as a warning against self-reliance and trusting one's own mind apart from God's Word — a Reformed emphasis on the noetic effects of sin and the necessity of Scripture.

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik's commentary (widely used in charismatic circles) is broadly evangelical but emphasizes the active, present work of the Holy Spirit (e.g., on v.6: the scoffer does not seek wisdom "in the teaching of God's Spirit") and practical application for church life, including warnings against hyper-regulation that quenches spiritual vitality (v.4).
